title: Unit 1: Polynomial and Rational Functions

topics.name: Rates of change

guide.title: Polynomial and rational functions: review guide
guide.intro: This unit is about how outputs change as inputs change, and about two function families: polynomials and rational functions. You read rates of change from tables and graphs, predict a graph's shape from its formula, and judge when a model makes sense.

sections.title: Rates of change
body: The average rate of change of f on [a, b] is (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a): the slope of the line through the two points. A positive rate means the function increased over the interval; a negative rate means it decreased.
When the average rates over consecutive equal intervals are increasing, the graph is concave up. When they are decreasing, it is concave down.
points: Linear functions have a constant rate of change: constant first differences in a table with equal input steps.
Quadratic functions have rates of change that change at a constant rate: constant second differences.
Where the rate of change switches sign, the function has a relative maximum or minimum. Where the concavity changes, it has a point of inflection.
equations: average rate of change of f on [a, b]

sections.title: Zeros, end behavior, asymptotes, and holes
body: A polynomial's end behavior comes from its leading term axⁿ. Even degree means both ends go the same way; odd degree means they go opposite ways. The sign of a decides which way.
A rational function r(x) = p(x)/q(x) is undefined where q(x) = 0. Factor first: a factor that cancels completely leaves a hole, and a factor left in the denominator gives a vertical asymptote.
points: A degree-n polynomial has exactly n complex zeros counted with multiplicity, at most n real zeros, and at most n − 1 turning points.
At a real zero of even multiplicity the graph touches the x-axis and turns around. At odd multiplicity it crosses.
When the coefficients are real, nonreal zeros come in conjugate pairs a ± bi.

Rational end behavior: if the numerator has lower degree, y = 0 is the horizontal asymptote; if the degrees are equal, y = (ratio of leading coefficients); if the numerator's degree is one higher, there is a slant asymptote, found by polynomial division.
A hole appears at x = c when (x − c) has at least as high a multiplicity in the numerator as in the denominator.

sections.title: Building and judging models
body: Choose a model from the data or the situation. Constant first differences suggest linear, constant second differences suggest quadratic, and a quantity that levels off toward a value suggests a rational function with a horizontal asymptote.

Every model has a domain that makes sense in context (a length cannot be negative, a time starts at 0) and assumptions (for example, no air resistance). Predictions outside that domain are not reliable.
points: Transformations: g(x) = a·f(b(x − h)) + k stretches vertically by a factor of |a|, horizontally by a factor of 1/|b|, and shifts the graph h right and k up.
State the domain restriction and the units with any answer from a model.
Piecewise functions model situations whose rule changes partway, such as a rate that changes after a limit is reached.

example.prompt: Find the holes, vertical asymptotes, and horizontal asymptote of r(x) = (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6).
example.solution: Factor: r(x) = (x − 3)(x + 3) / ((x + 3)(x − 2)). The factor x + 3 cancels completely, so there is a hole at x = −3; its y-value is (−3 − 3)/(−3 − 2) = 6/5. The factor x − 2 stays in the denominator, so x = 2 is a vertical asymptote. The degrees are equal and both leading coefficients are 1, so y = 1 is the horizontal asymptote.

misconceptions: “Every zero of the denominator is a vertical asymptote.”
If the factor cancels completely with the numerator, the graph has a hole there instead.
“A graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote.”
A horizontal asymptote describes end behavior only; the graph may cross it at moderate x-values.
“The average rate of change is the average of the two outputs.”
It is the change in output divided by the change in input.
“A model that fits the data works for every input.”
Use it only on the domain that makes sense in context, and say what it assumes.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x² + 1, what is the average rate of change of f on the interval [1, 3]?
choiceExplanations: 8 is the change in f, 10 − 2, but it was not divided by the change in x, 3 − 1 = 2.
5 comes from f(3)/(3 − 1) = 10/2; the starting value f(1) must be subtracted first.
1/4 is (3 − 1)/(10 − 2), the change in x over the change in f: the ratio is upside down.

questions.prompt: A table gives g(0) = 3, g(1) = 5, g(2) = 9, g(3) = 15, and g(4) = 23. Which type of function of lowest degree fits these values exactly?
questions.explanation: First differences are 2, 4, 6, 8, and the second differences are all 2. Constant second differences with equal input steps mean a quadratic fits exactly: g(x) = x² + x + 3.
choiceExplanations: A linear function needs constant first differences, but these are 2, 4, 6, 8.
An exponential function needs a constant ratio between consecutive outputs, but 5/3 and 9/5 are not equal.
A cubic needs nonzero constant third differences. Here the third differences are 0, so a quadratic, which has lower degree, already fits exactly.

questions.prompt: Over consecutive input intervals of equal length, a function's average rates of change are 6, 4, 3, and 1. Which describes the function over this whole span?
questions.explanation: All the rates are positive, so the function is increasing. The rates are getting smaller, so the graph bends downward: concave down.
choiceExplanations: Concave up would need the rates to be getting larger, not smaller.
Positive rates of change mean the function is increasing, not decreasing.
Positive rates mean increasing, and shrinking rates mean concave down, not up.

questions.prompt: What is the end behavior of p(x) = −2x⁵ + 7x² − 1?
choices: As x → ∞ and as x → −∞, p(x) → −∞
As x → ∞ and as x → −∞, p(x) → ∞
questions.explanation: The leading term −2x⁵ controls the end behavior. Odd degree means the ends go in opposite directions, and the negative coefficient means the graph falls to the right and rises to the left.
choiceExplanations: This is the end behavior for a positive leading coefficient, such as 2x⁵.
Both ends going the same way happens with even degree; the degree here is 5.
Both ends rising happens with even degree and a positive leading coefficient; this polynomial has odd degree and a negative leading coefficient.

questions.prompt: For p(x) = (x − 1)²(x + 3), what happens to the graph at its x-intercepts?
choices: It crosses the x-axis at x = 1 and touches it at x = −3
It touches the x-axis at x = 1 and crosses it at x = −3
It crosses the x-axis at both x = 1 and x = −3
It touches the x-axis at both x = 1 and x = −3
questions.explanation: x = 1 is a zero of multiplicity 2 (even), so p does not change sign there: the graph touches the axis and turns. x = −3 has multiplicity 1 (odd), so p changes sign: the graph crosses.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the multiplicities: x − 1 is squared and x + 3 is not.
At x = 1 the factor is squared, so p does not change sign there and the graph cannot cross.
At x = −3 the factor appears once, so p changes sign and the graph crosses.

questions.prompt: Which describes the graph of r(x) = (x² − 4)/(x² − x − 2)?
choices: Vertical asymptotes at x = 2 and x = −1
A hole at x = 2 and a vertical asymptote at x = −1
A hole at x = −1 and a vertical asymptote at x = 2
A vertical asymptote at x = −1 and no hole
questions.explanation: Factor: r(x) = (x − 2)(x + 2) / ((x − 2)(x + 1)). The factor x − 2 cancels completely, leaving a hole at x = 2 (at y = 4/3). The factor x + 1 stays in the denominator, so x = −1 is a vertical asymptote.
choiceExplanations: x = 2 makes the denominator zero, but the same factor cancels with the numerator, so it is a hole, not an asymptote.
The roles are reversed: x − 2 cancels (a hole) and x + 1 stays in the denominator (an asymptote).
r is still undefined at x = 2 after the factor cancels, so the graph has a hole there.

questions.prompt: What is the slant asymptote of the graph of r(x) = (2x² + 3x − 1)/(x − 1)?
questions.explanation: Divide: 2x² + 3x − 1 = (x − 1)(2x + 5) + 4, so r(x) = 2x + 5 + 4/(x − 1). As x → ±∞, 4/(x − 1) → 0, so the graph approaches y = 2x + 5.
choiceExplanations: 2x is only the ratio of the leading terms; the division also produces the constant 5, which shifts the asymptote up.
A horizontal asymptote needs the numerator's degree to be at most the denominator's. Here it is one higher, so the asymptote is slanted.
2x + 3 copies the numerator's coefficients without dividing; the quotient of the division is 2x + 5.

questions.prompt: A polynomial with real coefficients has a zero at x = 1 of multiplicity 2 and a zero at x = 2 − i. What is the least possible degree of the polynomial?
questions.explanation: With real coefficients, nonreal zeros come in conjugate pairs, so 2 + i is also a zero. Counting multiplicity, the zeros include 1, 1, 2 − i, and 2 + i, so the degree is at least 4.
choiceExplanations: 3 counts the double zero but leaves out the conjugate zero 2 + i.
2 counts each listed zero once, ignoring both the multiplicity of x = 1 and the conjugate 2 + i.
5 would add a conjugate for the real zero 1, but a real number is its own conjugate.

questions.prompt: Squares of side x cm are cut from the corners of a 20 cm by 20 cm sheet, and the sides are folded up to make an open box with volume V(x) = x(20 − 2x)². Which domain makes sense for this model?
questions.explanation: x is a length, so x > 0, and a square is cut from both ends of each 20 cm side, so 2x < 20, that is, x < 10. At x = 0 or x = 10 the box has no volume.
choiceExplanations: Cutting x from both ends of a 20 cm side needs 2x < 20, so x cannot reach 20.
x > 0 ignores that the cuts cannot use up the whole side; for x ≥ 10 nothing is left to fold.
Negative or very large lengths have no meaning here, even though the formula accepts them.

questions.prompt: The average cost per item for producing n items is C(n) = (500 + 2n)/n dollars. What does the horizontal asymptote y = 2 mean in this context?
choices: As production grows, the average cost per item approaches $2
Producing 2 items gives the lowest average cost
For very large n, the average cost per item drops below $2
questions.explanation: C(n) = 500/n + 2. As n grows, the $500 fixed cost is spread over more items, so 500/n → 0 and the average cost approaches $2 per item from above.
choiceExplanations: $500 is the fixed cost; $2 is the added cost of each item.
A small n gives a large average cost because the fixed cost is shared by few items: C(2) = $252.
500/n is always positive, so C(n) stays above 2. It approaches 2 but never reaches or passes it.

questions.prompt: A ball's height in meters is modeled by h(t) = −4.9t² + 20t + 2, where t is the number of seconds after it is thrown. Over what interval of t is this model reasonable?
questions.explanation: The model applies from the throw until the ball lands, when h(t) = 0. Solving −4.9t² + 20t + 2 = 0 gives t = (20 + √439.2)/9.8 ≈ 4.18 s; the other solution is negative. After that the model predicts negative heights.
choiceExplanations: 2.04 s (t = 20/9.8) is when the ball reaches its highest point, not when it lands.
4.08 s solves −4.9t² + 20t = 0, which ignores the 2 m starting height.
For t > 4.18 the model gives negative heights, which cannot happen; the ball has already landed.
